quotes.verbatim_quote:
Sometimes a walking bass style is used (first two measures) and sometimes a measure

has a riff while the melody is not active.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the two distinct bass-line strategies and signals when each applies relative to melody activity.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
With the addition of the major and minor third as harmony indicator, this tune is more

sophisticated than earlier ones.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the core harmonic technique of using thirds in the bass to signal chord quality, marking a conceptual step up.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This final tune, a bebop blues, also uses root, fifth, major and minor thirds in the bass. This
makes the harmony much richer. The melody is more active, so the bass moves with longer value
quotes.why_load_bearing: Articulates the rule that a more active melody necessitates longer bass note values -- a key voice-leading trade-off.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The arpeggio (‘little harp”), as an accompanying technique, is a guitar “natural.” If you began
playing fingerstyle guitar to accompany a singer—perhaps yourself—then you already have used
arpeggios for accompanying. These fingerpicking patterns using the individual notes of chords
are referred to as “broken chords.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Formally defines the arpeggio technique and its alternate name broken chords, grounding the terminology for Part 5.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Arpeggiation accompaniment works well as a faster flow of notes (eighth or sixteenth notes)
accompanying a slower melody made up of whole, half, and quarter notes. There are no fixed
rules, however.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives the practical guideline for matching arpeggio rhythm to melody rhythm while warning against absolutes.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The right-hand fingering for the arpeggiation above is typical. When the arpeggio lies across
several strings—as it does most often—p plays the lower string(s), while /and m play the middle
and higher strings. Use a free stroke as you progress with i, mand a, from low strings to high, and
you will not inadvertently damp the jower strings.

Since p, i, and m are occupied playing the arpeggios, use the a finger, rest stroke, for the
melody when needed.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Core right-hand technique rule for fingerstyle arpeggio accompaniment, specifying finger assignments and stroke types.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Sustain the arpeggio note group by holding the left-hand fingers in place.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Essential left-hand rule that produces the characteristic harp-like resonance of arpeggiated accompaniment.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Arpeggios can be played in a detached, separated manner, with no notes melding together. On
guitar, this usually happens more often in single note melody lines, not as an accompanying device.
Therefore, you must use your taste and experience to decide when and where to sustain the broken
chord and when to purposely separate the notes.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the alternate arpeggiation style and frames the choice between sustain and separation as musical judgment.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
watch that your choice of arpeggiation doesn’t reach higher than the
melody, which might obscure the melody and confuse the listener.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Critical voice-leading rule: accompaniment must stay below the melody to preserve melodic clarity.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
If you set up an arpeggiated upward sweep from the sixth string toward the first as the primary
pattern, keep it going as best you can. If you run out of room because the melody is slow, insert
some passing tones between the existing lower notes to stretch it out rather than change the
direction of the pattern.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Specific problem-solving technique for preserving arpeggio pattern consistency when melody occupies too much range.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
You may find it impossible to sustain every note of the arpeggio because of fingering problems,
such as having to play two consecutive notes on one string. Go for the overall effect, and don’t
get crazy over the shorter duration of a single note.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Pragmatic technical rule: prioritize musical effect over mechanical perfection when fingering conflicts with sustain.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
If you notice that the melody of the tune you wish to arrange continually leaps up and down
wildly, abandon arpeggiation for that particular tune and choose another accompaniment
technique.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Clear decision rule for when arpeggio technique is inappropriate, teaching students to match technique to melodic character.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A simple way of harmonizing the melody is to use a note that is three scale steps below the
melody.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the diatonic-thirds harmonization technique that is the central concept of Part 6.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Usually the way to pluck a strong melody line is to use rest strokes as much as possible. Since
thirds are on adjacent strings, the free stroke must be used. To make the top melody note louder,
just do it. lsolate the highest string and tug at it more forcefully than the lower string of the chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explains the key technical constraint of playing parallel thirds on adjacent strings and the technique for projecting the melody.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
For this first example, you may use pand /together. Then try mand atogether,
which is what you will need when you add the thumb soon.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Prescribes the two right-hand finger pairings for parallel thirds and anticipates the next arranging step.
